summary: Reliance includes Jio mobile and broadband, shops and online retail, media, fuels and industrial materials, oil and gas production, and projects to make solar and energy-storage equipment.
description: A household may pay for a Jio connection or buy something from a group shop. A factory may buy materials that Reliance makes from oil. These businesses serve different needs: putting them under the same group does not make their costs or ways of earning the same.
money: Customers pay for goods, connectivity, content or industrial supplies. The group pays for crude oil and other inputs, shop stock, workers, networks, factories, delivery and content. It also spends to build new capacity. A sale or subscription has to cover the relevant costs before it contributes profit.
customers: Mobile and broadband subscribers, retail shoppers, media subscribers and advertisers, and companies buying fuels, chemicals, materials or oil and gas. The paying customer and the product supplied differ across these businesses.
drivers: Demand, selling prices compared with input costs, repeat shoppers and subscribers, use of plants and networks, and the spending required to maintain or expand them.

groups.title: Fuels and materials made from oil
groups.examples: Transportation fuels, materials used to make plastics, and polyester-related materials.
groups.explanation: A refinery processes crude oil into products such as transport fuels. Chemical plants make materials that other manufacturers use. A material buyer pays for the specified product; the company must cover crude or other inputs and the cost of operating its plants.

groups.title: Oil and gas taken from underground
groups.examples: The separate oil-and-gas exploration and production business.
groups.explanation: Exploration means looking for deposits; production means extracting and supplying oil or gas. This differs from buying crude and processing it. What can be extracted, at what cost, and the selling price affect the business.

groups.title: Shopping in stores or online
groups.examples: Grocery, electronics, fashion, beauty and other retail formats.
groups.explanation: Imagine a customer buying food or a phone. The retailer buys or arranges merchandise, keeps stock, serves the customer and delivers where needed. The selling price must cover the goods as well as shops, staff, storage and other costs.

groups.title: Jio connections and digital services
groups.examples: Mobile service, home broadband and business digital services.
groups.explanation: The customer pays for a connection or service. The network needs equipment, maintenance and permission to use radio frequencies, called spectrum. Adding users helps only if their payments support service and investment costs.

groups.title: Media: content and audiences
groups.examples: JioStar, studio, news and related media operations within the group’s stated structure.
groups.explanation: Viewers may pay for access to programmes, while advertisers pay to reach audiences. Making programmes or buying the right to show them costs money. The group can share ownership with partners, so check which company’s business is being described.

groups.title: New energy: developing equipment and production
groups.examples: Solar manufacturing, energy storage and green-hydrogen-related development.
groups.explanation: Solar panels help generate electricity and storage equipment holds energy for later use. Green hydrogen means hydrogen made using renewable electricity. Building these capabilities is followed by testing, regular production and finding paying customers; an announced project is not already a successful operating business.

basics.title: A higher selling price does not always mean more profit
basics.text: If crude oil costs more, the fuels made from it may sell for more too. What matters is the relationship between the cost of inputs and the price of outputs, together with the cost of running the plants.

basics.title: One group can contain partly owned companies
basics.text: A subsidiary is a company the group controls. Some businesses also have outside investors or are owned jointly with partners. Their arrangements affect what is included in the accounts and how much profit belongs to the parent company’s owners.

steps.title: Build or arrange what the business needs
steps.text: Operate plants, networks, stores or content services appropriate to the customer’s need.

steps.title: Produce goods or deliver a service
steps.text: Process inputs, stock merchandise, provide connectivity or make content available.

steps.title: Receive purchases, orders or subscriptions
steps.text: Supply the customer and record the sale or service under its terms. Some customers pay immediately; other business sales have agreed payment dates.

steps.title: Pay costs and fund future work
steps.text: Cover inputs, staff and other running bills, then meet maintenance, expansion and financing commitments. The group must decide which businesses receive more investment.

specifics.title: Refining and extracting oil are different businesses
specifics.text: A producer benefits differently from a price change than a plant buying crude to make fuel. Read each activity’s costs and selling conditions instead of assuming all oil-related businesses move together.

specifics.title: A busy shop and a busy network need different checks
specifics.text: For retail, ask whether customers buy enough stock to cover shop and delivery costs. For Jio, ask whether subscriber payments cover service and network needs. Registered accounts or visitor counts alone do not answer either question.

specifics.title: A new project needs more than an opening announcement
specifics.text: Building a factory is followed by testing, regular production, acceptable quality and customer purchases. Starting operations does not by itself show that the investment has earned its cost back.

watch: What is changing the earnings from fuels and materials?
Input prices and product prices can move differently.

Read plant activity, input costs, product selling prices and the company’s explanation of what remains between them. Keep extracting oil or gas separate from processing bought crude into fuels and materials.
Do Jio customers support the cost of the network?
More subscribers still require reliable service and investment.

Read active customers, payments per user on the stated basis, service costs and network spending. Check spectrum payment commitments and equipment costs rather than treating a headline earnings measure as freely available cash.
Are stores and online retail selling stock usefully?
More outlets can add costs as well as customers.

Read sales per store where disclosed, product types, unsold stock and running costs. Check whether quoted sales include tax and whether the business needs extra storage, delivery or promotional spending.
What stage have media and new-energy changes reached?
A new partnership or factory changes more than a brand name.

Check which company owns the operation, what partners own and whether comparisons cover the same businesses. For new factories, distinguish plans and construction from actual products sold to customers.
Can the group fund several businesses at once?
Factories, shops, networks and content can all require money.

Read cash from operating businesses alongside investment, borrowing, shop rentals and spectrum commitments. Check amounts owed to other owners and future spending promises before treating a headline profit figure as cash available to distribute.
risks: Input prices or demand turn unfavourable
Fuel and material prices can leave less after buying inputs and running plants.
Factories, networks and shops can use cash before sales cover their costs.
Retail, connectivity and media need useful selection, reliable service and workable prices.
Group arrangements become hard to compare
Acquisitions, partnerships and partly owned companies can change which sales and earnings belong in each reported figure.
context: Follow the customer’s payment through the relevant business

A Jio recharge pays for connectivity, a shop purchase pays for merchandise, and an industrial order pays for specified materials. Start with that job and its costs, then use the final financial section to compare the activities without adding overlapping group figures.
quiz: Can sales numbers from every Reliance business presentation simply be added together?
Not safely. They can use different definitions, include transactions within the group or cover different companies. Use the group’s own reconciliation to avoid counting the same activity twice.

financialNotes.title: These are selected business highlights
financialNotes.text: The verified table is a set of report business highlights, not a full consolidated revenue or profit reconciliation. Retail uses the report’s value-of-sales presentation. The rows must not be treated as exact shares of group revenue.

financialNotes.title: EBITDA is not net profit or shareholder cash
financialNotes.text: The earnings column is EBITDA. Depreciation, financing, tax, ownership interests and investment needs matter afterward. Oil to Chemicals leads the displayed revenue, while Digital Services leads the displayed EBITDA; those answer different questions.
